sources.author: Entry entered by Adrija Mukherjee; Creator field names Hem Chandra Das Gupta
sources.publisher: Ancient Indian Boardgames: Digital Documentation; supported by Centre for Studies in Social Sciences, Calcutta and funded by JPN National Centre for Excellence, IIT Indore
sources.date_limit: Undated item. Embedded screenshot filename is not an article publication date.
sources.access: Full original-project mirror text inspected through web open. Main host timed out for coordinator. No downloaded capture claimed.
supported_claims: The entry identifies the game with Odisha and attributes its account to Das Gupta and an Odisha informant.
Two players control four tigers and twenty goats respectively.
Its Rules field describes play on a five-by-five array of intersections, with diagonal lines in each quadrant; pieces move along board lines to adjacent vacant points.
Four goats start on the board; the remaining sixteen are placed one at a time before goats may move. Tigers move first and alone capture by jumping a goat to a vacant point beyond.
This modern Rules field states all-goats capture as the tiger victory condition; goats win by immobilizing tigers.
limits: This is a documented version, not a claim of uniform rules throughout Odisha.
The enormous alternative-title list groups related games; do not treat every listed name as an exact synonym.
Do not attribute the modern all-goats criterion verbatim to the1926 author.
The Rights field says only Creative Commons without a specific licence. Do not reuse its image or prose.

draft_guidance: Aim for a compact original essay; source volume does not require450–650words. Focus on contrasting goals, how placement makes empty points matter, ordinary stones and a named photographic occasion, then the two documented endpoints. Avoid repeating source exposition or writing an unsupported complete rulebook. Ask players to agree their version before a game as editorial advice, not ethnographic fact. Footnotes should identify the modern sources actually inspected; historical citation remains mediated. No source photograph or article prose copied.
